utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody, and good morning to you, Madam Registrar. If you could kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are present. From amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bourgon. Prosecution is Mr. Thayer, Mr. Nicholls, Ms. Soljan; and Mr. McCloskey, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He was unable to be here this morning, Your Honour. He might be here later, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Before we bring in the witness, there are a few preliminaries. There is a Prosecution motion which was filed last Friday for leave to amend the 65 ter exhibit list with seven exhibits pertaining to Witness 100. Is there a position that you take, Defence teams? I'm asking you to respond now because there is very limited time. Basically, this is the problem that we have, and the documents themselves don't seem to be that dramatic. I'm choosing that word. And please, Mr. -- whoever is responsible for this. I know that Mr. McCloskey is not here, but we would have preferred if this motion had been filed some days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I'm responsible for that. I apologise for that. I handed out copies of the documents to my friends during the session on Friday, at the first break, I think, and explained that I would be filing a motion shortly. So I tried to give them more notice. I talked to my friends. I'm not sure there is an objection. I haven't heard one yet. I am sorry about the late filing of that. As you stated, the documents are not dramatic in the sense that they are all linked in or referred to things which are very clearly put forth in his interview. Two of them were used in the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As I say, please try to do your utmost to file such motions as early as possible. This weekend, it didn't matter much for us because we were meeting to decide on the various issues that were raised last week; and, very soon, we'll be coming down with our decision which engaged us in discussions over the Friday, as well as the weekend. But in future, please try to do your utmost. Do I take it that there is no objection? Okay. So the motion is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I thank my friends for that, and your point is well taken, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then there is another motion for protective measures for Witness 116, who will be coming here to testify pretty soon. He or she, so I don't give an indication, already testified in another case, in the Milosevic trial; and in that case, this witness was granted pseudonym, voice, and face distortion. So, essentially, those protective measures still continue to remain in force until or unless they are modified. So if perhaps the -- no one has any particular reason for seeking the modification of these protective measures, we can proceed to grant the motion. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. We did have the opportunity yesterday of discussing this, and the application for protective measures will be resisted and we will be applying for the existing order for protective measures in the Milosevic case, I think dated the 21st of November 2003, to be rescinded. Again, you might properly comment that this is an application that's being brought very late. It's based on information that's four years old, and this witness's testimony has now been scheduled four times in this case: October of last year, May of this year, June of this year, July of this year, and, finally, Wednesday of this week. It's somewhat startling that, even though we only sat for one session on Friday, nobody did us the courtesy of letting us know that this motion was going to land later that day. I've had the opportunity of speaking to Mr. Nicholls; and in the absence of Mr. McCloskey today, it is a bit of a problem because some of the underlying material in the Milosevic decision is very difficult for us to get hold of. We haven't actually been able to get hold of in the time frame a copy of the Trial Chamber's decision in Milosevic, and there were, in fact, two. And we haven't been able to get hold of the confidential annexes to the Prosecution's motion for protective measures in that case; and until we have those in our possession, we will be somewhat restricted in the arguments we can put before the Court. But to put you on notice, the central thrust will be that as a matter of public policy, this witness, who has given evidence about the facts of this case openly, previously, and was given protective measures in the Milosevic case in relation to evidence of a wholly different nature, ought not to be given protective measures in this case; and, secondly, that the circumstances which led to him being given protective measures in 2003 no longer obtain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think to cut matters short, I'm perfectly well aware what Mr. McCloskey is likely to be doing today and I have no wish to interrupt him in doing that, and I think we feel the best thing would be to schedule any discussion on this topic for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So this matter is being postponed until tomorrow morning. Now, we promised you last Friday that we'll avail ourselves of the time we had left that day, plus any further time needed, to consider and dispose of the various issues that were raised in the course of the week. We are going to deal with these issues orally, one by one. One of these issues was raised by all the Defence teams in a joint motion of the 12th of September, which was responded to orally by the Prosecution the following day or the day after, and I am going to begin with it. This joint Defence motion seeks clarification of the Trial Chamber's 9th March 2007 oral ruling on the application of Rule 65 ter. The Trial Chamber is somewhat puzzled as to why you felt there is any need for clarification of this particular ruling. The oral decision referred to in the joint Defence motion explicitly states: "Material identified for use in redirect need not be included in the 65 ter list or be given a 65 ter number before it is made use of." Perhaps the confusion that you seem to have or indicate that you had in your mind arises from looking and concentrating on another statement of this Trial Chamber in the same decision but which related to something completely different and certainly not the use of 65 ter documents during redirect. In our decision, there was no suggestion by the Trial Chamber that for the document to be used, a showing had to be made by the Prosecution that the cross-examination could not reasonably have been anticipated. The decision is unqualified and without condition. As stated previously, it is a general principle that will apply across the board both to the Prosecution and to the Defence later on. As to any surprise - and surprise is being made use of in quotes - that may result on the application of this decision, the Trial Chamber will consider on a case-by-case basis any representations that they were unaware of evidence to be adduced. The specific case cited by the Defence in relation to Witness 101 illustrates that points. Therefore, the Trial Chamber can see no need to address that matter by way of a general ruling, as each circumstance will be considered individually; and, indeed, last week we did have some instances where precisely we did that. On this basis, the relief sought by the Defence in the joint motion is hereby denied. Impeachment of a party's own witness. You will recall that this was debated last Friday as well, and we promised to determine it. As you are aware, this issue is not a new one in these proceedings, and I'll be coming to that very shortly. If there was any uncertainty, we wish to make it clear that the decision that we took in the case of Witness Simanic, to which reference was made last Friday by Mr. McCloskey and also by one or more members of the Defence teams, we wish to make it clear that this decision was not particular to the circumstances of that witness and his questionable status as a Prosecution, Defence, or Chamber witness. The majority of the Chamber, with myself dissenting, is of the opinion that it is open to any party to challenge the credibility of his or her witness in part or in full. The reasons for this position are set out clearly in the separate opinion of my colleague, Judge Kwon, of the 29th of April 2004 related to the Trial Chamber's confidential decision of the 20th January, 2004, in the case of the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic, and there is no point in repeating the same case here. Suffice it to say that the majority of Judges in this case is of the view that in a Tribunal of this nature, where professional Judges decide on matters of fact and law, the old-fashioned or maybe archaic rules prohibiting or restricting the impeachment of one's own witness, applicable in some common law jurisdictions, have no application here. Quite simply, as outlined by my colleague Judge Kwon in his earlier dissenting opinion, none of the reasons underlying those rules are valid in this Tribunal. In the opinion of the majority, it is for each party to determine to what extent and in what the credibility of a witness is to be challenged, and they clearly take the at their own peril; but in the end, the Chamber by majority is satisfied of their capability to assess the credibility of the witness in whole or in part based on the examinations conducted. As to my position in dissent, I have previously decided or participated in decisions on this identical issue in practically all the cases that I have been involved, particularly in Brdjanin and Oric, and I stand by the position I took in that instance. So you know now where you stand in relation to impeachment of one's own witness. Now, in the course of last week, there was another issue raised relating to 65 ter list documents. So the above decisions obviously impact directly on the objections advanced by the Defence to the admissibility of documents used by the Prosecution in the redirect examination of witnesses, and you will recall that we have postponed the admission of some of the documents precisely pending the determination of the motion, the joint motion, and also the issue of whether one is allowed to impeach his own witness. What we are going to add now is that to the extent that the objections rested on the 65 ter list, or the use of these documents in impeaching the credibility of a witness, as a logical consequence of what we have decided earlier today, the Trial Chamber now dismisses the particular objections; and to be more specific, I'm referring to the documents that were used during the testimony of Milomir Savcic and Nedeljko Trkulja. As to the fact that the witnesses in some instances claimed no knowledge of particular documents or even in some cases of the matters described therein, we believe that this does not preclude admission of such documents as a general principle. There still may be very relevant for assessing the credibility of the witness or other purposes. There may, of course, be individual cases where the nature of the documents and the witness's testimony is such that there is a particular argument against admissibility; for example, on the basis of relevance. But that would need to be determined on a case-by-case basis. In this instance, again, I repeat, therefore in relation only to witnesses Milomir Savcic and Nedeljko Trkulja, we are satisfied that the documents preferred by the Prosecution are admissible, and we order accordingly in favour of their admission. Mr. Josse, in the course of last week, raised the matter relating to document P528, which is a United Nations report on Srebrenica, which bears a date of 15th October 1999. The Prosecution seeks to tender this document, and we heard extensive submissions on this matter last Friday. The UN report on Srebrenica is an extensive report issued by the United Nations, as I said, in 1999, regarding the events surrounding the fall of Srebrenica. Some Defence teams, particularly the ones of General Gvero and also General Miletic, have opposed the admission of this document for reasons outlined during the oral debate, oral argument. We have given this a lot of thought, and our participation in the oral argument gave an early indication that we will be engaging ourselves in deep thought on this issue. We do not believe that there is anything in the nature of this document which makes it inadmissible before the Chamber, and we note that it has indeed been received by other Trial Chambers in previous cases dealing with Srebrenica, the Srebrenica events. However, in our view, it is a question of relevance in terms of the specific use to be made of it by the Chamber that matters. As with other documents, any of the parties may choose to use selected portions of this report with witnesses in either direct or cross-examination, use which could lead to the introduction of those parts of the report as evidence in the proceedings. Further, we are aware that at least General Smith and Richard Butler, future witnesses in these proceedings, have relied upon this document in the preparation of their own reports, which are to be proffered to the Trial Chamber. Obviously, at some point, it may become necessary for the Chamber to review those parts of the report referenced by these two individuals and perhaps other parts, too, to be able to properly assess their evidence. Finally, it is open to any of the parties to introduce selected portions of this document from the bar table for particular purposes that the party specifies in introducing the document. We do not, however, think or believe that it would be useful to this Trial Chamber for the entire document to be before us for unspecified purposes as sought by the Prosecution. We agree with the Defence submission that this would leave them in a position of doubt as to the use to be made by the Chamber of this extensive report which covers a myriad of issues. While the parties may wish to consider agreeing on the submission of selected portions, we do not consider that to be mandatory. As indicated, any of the parties may make a submission for the admission of any part of the report by justifying its relevance and probative value on any particular point. And that disposes of the issues we had before us in the course of last week. Any preliminaries that you wish to raise? Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Simply, Your Honour, that I think the next witness should be advised of his rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cautioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- yes, under Rule 90, and I have told him that that was likely and have explained the rule to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no protective measures, are there? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrbic, and welcome to this Tribunal. Very soon you're going to give evidence; but before you do so, we need to have you undertake by means of a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Nicholls will be the first one to ask you questions. He will then be followed by the various Defence teams or some of them. However, before you start giving evidence, my attention has been drawn that since you lived a part of these events, it would be better if I alerted you to a particular right that you enjoy under our Rules. And that relates to an individual's right not to be forced to incriminate himself by answering questions. There is the possibility, although I am not saying that this will happen, that questions may be put to you which, if you answer truthfully, could expose you possibly to criminal proceedings. I know this has been explained to you, but it's my responsibility as the Presiding Judge to explain it again to you. In such cases, you have a right to address the Trial Chamber, the four of us up here, and seek an exemption from answering such questions. Of course, we will hear what you have to say; and if we are convinced that it's the case of exempting you, we will grant you such exemption. However, we also have the absolute discretion not agree with granting the requested exemption and, rather, decide to force you, to compel you, to answer such questions. If we do that, you enjoy a further right, and that being the following: Unless in answering such questions you have committed false testimony, then whatever you state in answering those questions cannot be used and will not be used against you in any future proceedings that may be instituted. Have I been clear in explaining this to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Major General, and I'm going now to pass you into the hands of Mr. Nicholls. You still estimate an hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think it will less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I am Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your current occupation, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I am a retired general, so I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Where were you born, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Hotkovci, Glamoc municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what is the date of your birth?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20 October 1946.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you are Bosnian Serb; is that how you would describe your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As I told you when I met you on Saturday, I will try to not keep you in that chair for any longer than necessary, so I'd like to go to our topics as quickly and concisely as we can. And the first one of those is your military background. Correct me if I'm wrong in any of these statements I'm going to make. In 1966, you went to the military academy in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In 1965. That's when I started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long were you at the academy?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was at the academy in Belgrade for two years; then I continued for one year in Zadar at the anti-aircraft academy; and then I returned to Batajnica, where I completed my military academy education in 1968, graduating from the rocket school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what was next in your career, military career?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the units of air -- Anti-Aircraft Defence in the vicinity of Belgrade. There I stayed until 1981. Do you want me to give you any details about my duties and tasks or not? Then I went to the high military political school to complete that school, and I completed that school and I remained teaching there. My subject was the dialectic of society which was actually a philosophy subject. That was the course that I was teaching. In 1985, I was transferred to the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, to the Administration for Moral Guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then if you could just continue briefly, take us through to 1993, if you can just briefly describe your positions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I shall do it straight away. After the reorganisation of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the political administration from that Secretariat was reorganised into the Administration for Moral Guidance affiliated with the General Staff. That's how I ended up with the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia. I was in that administration, the chief of the first section, the section for Moral Guidance. I remained there until 1993. In 1993 for a brief period of time, I was the chief, i.e., the director, of the Military Publication Centre, until the moment I joined the army of Republika Srpska which was on the 17th of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us which -- what position you held in the VRS and in which corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I joined the 2nd Krajina Corps. I was assistant commander of that corps for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs, and I stayed in that position until the 24th of July, I believe that it was then, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you for one moment. Why did you -- if you can explain, why did you go to the 2nd Krajina Corps? Why that particular location?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That's how I was assigned when I reported to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is it also in the area where you were born, that corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The command post of the 2nd Krajina Corps was at Ostrelj near Drvar, which is some 70 kilometres away from my native village, from Glamoc; maybe not exactly 70 kilometres, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, continue, please. What happened to you, you were going to tell us, in July 1994?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I received information that I should report urgently to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska to be reassigned to a new duty. When I arrived at the Main Staff, I was told that I would be proposed to be promoted to the post of the assistant commander for Organisation, Mobilisation, and Personnel matters, and that's what happened. I was appointed because all appointments that required a person to have the rank of a general is within the purview of the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And when were you promoted to general in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was on the 23rd of June 1995. Any general has to spend some time performing duties requiring the ranks of a colonel in order to gain some experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you resign or leave the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of December 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then what's the next step in your career? Where do you go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was still not fulfilling conditions for retirement, and that's why I remained without any assignments in the army of Yugoslavia; and then when I was up for retirement, I was eventually retired in 2001. That's when I fulfilled all the conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so after December 1996, where did you go physically? Did you stay in the RS, or did you go to Belgrade? Where were you living?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you retired in 2001, what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just say for the record I see that you have a document in front of you and a note pad. Could you just tell us - I think I see what it is - what you've brought into the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is a notebook that I received from you. It is clean. There is nothing in there. I prepared it just in case I had to make any notes, and this is a copy of my interview that I had with Mr. McCloskey in 2005 in Serbian language, and I have nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Just a pencil.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. If you want to refer to your interview, please let us know. Now, that transcript of your 2005 interview with the OTP, you reviewed that before you came here in your own language; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on Saturday, when you met with me, you made various corrections and comments to your -- to the interview; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go to July 1995, the time when you're an assistant commander in the Main Staff. I'd like you to very, very briefly tell the Trial Chamber what your main tasks were as assistant commander for Organisation, Mobilisation, and Personnel Affairs. If you could give us a brief description of your duties, and I mean as brief as you can make it and be accurate.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief but we are talking about a very broad area. I'll start with the Organisation. The Organisation of the army of Republika Srpska, when I first arrived, had already been established and I did not have much to do in that respect. As for the Mobilisation of the army, this pertained to my duties in the following respect: The requirements of the army for mobilisation of people and materiel were within my purview. However, the call-up papers, issuing call-up papers and calling on people to join the army, were within the purview of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. As for the Personnel affairs, they occupied most of my time, and let me just tell you briefly what they entailed: Education of officers and non-commissioned officers, assignment of officers, preparation of documents for their appointment to their establishment positions, preparation of documents for the promotion of the officers, preparation of documents for decorations, as well as the preparation of documents for reassignment from one unit to another. There may have been some other minor things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. On 11 July 1995, where were you posted?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I was in Han Pijesak at the rear command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who was your immediate superior at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: All the time, throughout the entire war, my superior was the commander of the Main Staff, not for a single moment did I have somebody else as my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: General Mladic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to now start talking about some documents with you, and the first one is 02899. Now, in a minute this document should appear on the screen in front of you in your language. If it doesn't, let me know. Excuse me. It may take a moment.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask something, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left screen, I have the English translation. Would that be customary in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it bother you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not at all, no, but I was just wondering. I understand English just a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the left scene, there is a transcript of what is being said now. Every single word that you say in Serbian is being translated to us into English; and for those of us who prefer French, in French. And, well, you have it there in front of you as well, and the transcript is only in English. You can't have it in Serbo-Croat. But if it bothers you, don't look at it. Concentrate on the other one, on the other monitor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not bothered. On the contrary, this is a good opportunity. It would be, if I had the time, to brush up on my English. Unfortunately, I don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest you concentrate on your testimony rather than brushing. Yes, let's go ahead. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, can you see that document in your language?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I apologise for this digression, first of all. Now I can see the document. I can see the number as well. I apologise. Let me just get hold of my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you prefer to have a copy of the document in paper in front of you, or can you see that clearly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No need for that. I apologise. No need for that because the copy on the screen is quite legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we scroll down so that the witness can see the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall, Witness, that we looked at this document together on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We saw it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go back up to the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We see here that at the top, on the third line on the left, the confidential number begins with 09. What does that 09 signify, which organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That number indicates the sector in which I was assistant commander for those affairs, so it belonged to the sector for Organisation, Mobilisation, and Personnel. Other numbers indicated other things. The 09 means affiliation to a certain sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that this document is dated 12th of July 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And your name, if we go down to the bottom again, appears on the bottom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall this document, drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did; but to tell you the truth, I can't see the initials clearly. It seems to indicate that somebody else drafted this but I believe I dictated those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Can you scroll up a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This document is addressed to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska with a request to requisition buses at the Secretariats enumerated here because they were in charge. They were responsible for ordering these Secretariats to requisition. Just a minute. It's about buses. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me read quickly what -- this is a short document. It states: "Order: As urgently as possible the Sarajevo and Zvornik MO Secretariats, to mobilise through the Pale, Sokolac, Rogatica, Visegrad, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, Milici, Bratunac, and Zvornik Ministry of Defence departments MO, all available buses in these municipalities. It is necessary to mobilise at least 50 buses which must be sent to Bratunac Sports Stadium by 1430 on 12 July 1995 at the latest." Now, it says: "Order: As urgently as possible." Is this an order or a request?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In wartime, it's difficult to find the right words, and sometimes inappropriate words slip in. What should be written here is that it is necessary to instruct Secretariats to do whatever, not order Secretariats, because it was their responsibility, and we were asking them to do so. But if you allow me one comment, it's not that I'm saying that Secretariats were free to ignore our requests, but we did not want to interfere in their jurisdiction, the jurisdiction of National Defence Secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Well, we'll look at some other documents soon and see how they perceived this document which says "Order" on it. Who told you to direct this order, or however you want to characterise it, to the MOD? How did you get the information which you passed on here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I received that information by telephone; but for the life of me, I can't remember who passed it on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But when I--

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: After that, I also used the phone to call the Ministry of Defence to tell them it's necessary to requisition these buses, and the person who answered my call at the Ministry of Defence said that I should put it in writing without fail, and I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When did you receive that telephone call?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it was sometime in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And on which day? On the 12th when this order was drafted, or on another day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, it was during the night, so I suppose it was the night of the 11th because, as you see, this document was written on the 12th. That means the previous night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, on 11th you said you were at Han Pijesak. Do you know where that telephone call came from; in other words, where it originated from?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember which body of the VRS gave you this information to pass on?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you to look at your statement, if I may, on page 24 at lines 2 to 9. You find that, and I'll read out the question and answer that might help you. Question - this is page 24 as well of the English - "Did you know that his," I think it should be this, "or his request of 12 July came from Ratko Mladic?" And your answer was: "Indirectly through somebody." That's around line 8 of yours.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And on page 25 of the English, which is also on page 24 of yours, at lines 28 to 32, you were asked: "You are passing on Mladic's order?" And your answer was: "That must have been or he -- that was his request, his demand." Do you remember saying that in the interview?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I do. I remember saying that and I stand by it. Should I repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. You don't need to repeat it, thank you, if you stand by it. Now, at this time, on the 11th, when you got this information and that you were to pass on this order, or on the 12th, what did you know or what were you told these buses were to be used for, these buses that are to be sent to Bratunac stadium?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As soon as it was said that buses were needed, I knew that they were needed to transport people but I didn't know which people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "people"? What kind of people are you talking about? Soldiers? Civilians? What?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: During the war, we used buses to transport our personnel, our fighting men, or we used trucks. This time, I was told that such a large number of buses was needed for an evacuation. But an evacuation of whom or what, nobody said anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you know that day what was happening? That day, the 11th and 12th, did you know what was happening in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you another document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 12, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take a look at this document, sir. Do you remember we looked at this one as well on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We looked at it together. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a document dated 12 July 1995, "Secretariat of the Defence Ministry, Sarajevo. Subject: Request for mobilisation of buses." I'll just read the beginning part: "Pursuant to a request by the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army," and then it's got the number 0931-12-3154 dated 12 July 1995, regarding the mobilisation of buses. "Immediately mobilise at least 20 buses and drivers from the municipalities of Pale, Sokolac, Rogatica, and Han Pijesak. The drivers are to report with their buses to the Sports Stadium in Bratunac by 12 July 1995 at 1430 hours. Immediately send a report to this ministry about the actions taken in connection with the aforementioned request." Now, the number referenced in the first line, that's the same number as your order that we just looked at, is that right, the one that ends in 154?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is correct. We have discussed this before, sir. You see the wording, "pursuant to the request." They don't say pursuant to an order. Maybe it's same in English; but in our language, there is a distinction. So it was clearly understood by the person who wrote this, and the number indicated is correct. We did the comparison yesterday or the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So, very briefly tell us, what is this document? What is this document attempting to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Ministry of Defence is responding to our request and immediately orders the Secretariat in Sarajevo to mobilise 20 buses, as I see now, according to their assessment, which means they were able to requisition that number, and they order the Secretariat to immediately report back. That would be a brief summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to look at now 65 ter 13, a similar document, dated 12 July 1995. This one Secretariat of the Defence Ministry, Zvornik. Take a moment to look at this document, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is another one that we looked at together on Saturday, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very briefly, as you did with the last one, can you just tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The same as with the previous document. The only difference is that the Secretariat of the Ministry of Defence of Zvornik is now reacting to the same document in the same way. Taking a look at the number of buses, it seems they had the ability to requisition 30 buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you answered this, but was the person you spoke to on the telephone, on the night of the 11th, Momcilo Kovacevic, the person who is signing this document and the last one?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The person I talked to is Momcilo Kovacevic, Momo Kovacevic. Could you raise it a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I think he signed it. No. This document is from the Zvornik Secretariat, and Momcilo Kovacevic signed the document. Right. That's him, Momcilo Kovacevic. And can you show the document of the Ministry of Defence, because I'm confused now. Could there be another Momcilo Kovacevic in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you'll see this one is signed for, and we'll keep going through some documents and maybe it will be clearer to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But it's true that I talked to Momcilo Kovacevic, who worked at the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to go to 65 ter number 14 now. Take a look and read this document which again is similar. Here, again, we have mobilisation of a minimum 50 buses including drivers to report immediately to the Sports Stadium in Bratunac, also dated 12 July 1995. And in the bottom, it states: "Keep this ministry regularly informed about the actions taken in connection with the aforementioned request." You recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I recognise the document. We looked at it recently, during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, again --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can note that it is related to the request from the Main Staff, and their number is correct. I wouldn't like to go into the further details and how they are responding. We can see that they are responding to the document of the Main Staff and taking the measures that they see fit; and, of course, they are required to report back to the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one is 65 ter number 15, now 13 July 1995, Secretariat of the Defence Ministry, Sarajevo. We looked at this document, sir. Very briefly, is this again connected to the Main Staff document that you authored and sent to Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This document does not mention the number of the request from the Main Staff; but in view of the text itself, it's obvious that this document, too, is related.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a couple more of these. 65 ter number 16; again, 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can see it. We reviewed it as well, together, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And this one is also related, is it not, to your document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now if we could go to 65 ter number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Take a look at this one, sir, from the 13th of July 1995, Secretariat of the Defence Ministry, Bijeljina. This one references the number from your order or request, as you call it, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And so, again, this document is, to be brief, a result of your order or your request, as you call it, to the MOD?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Look at the heading: "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence." So the Ministry of Defence authored this request for the Main Staff, and then they elaborated the details in their own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And it's pursuant to a request by the Main Staff, and then we see the same number that appears on the document you drafted, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have the break now, I just have a few more documents to organise that are related but a little bit different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have 65 ter number 13 back up, please, just for a moment. Thank you, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want us to look at this document, again, for a minute to make a note of the number at the top, 3615/95. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I have something to tell you now at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I brought into the courtroom another pair of glasses that would be more practical now because of the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you see the number at the top of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could now go to P02900, number 02900.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, this order to the Ministry of Defence departments in Zvornik, Milici, Vlasenica, Sekovici, and Bratunac, dated 12 July 1995, for bus drivers and buses to immediately go to the Sports Centre in Bratunac is another document we looked at Saturday, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: We've also seen that document on Saturday, I believe, but we didn't make out this word in the heading, "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence, Secretariat section," then we don't see the word; and then on the right-hand side we see, "Republika Srpska, Ministry of Defence, department of Zvornik." I don't know whose stamp is there on the left, but I can say that this is a response to all the other documents. Now it's in the purview of the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And there is no question in your mind -- well, is this an order? What is this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are issuing an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And it refers specifically and says that it is pursuant to the document we just looked at, 65 ter number 13, number 02-213615/95 also of 12 July, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct. This document invokes that document of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we could now look at 02901.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Quite similar, sir. Will you take a look at this document, also from the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We've reviewed this one, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, again, just as the last document we looked at, 02900, this order is directly in response to the previous order we looked at, 65 ter number 13. You can see the same number on the second line. It ends 3615/95.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: We established during proofing that the numbers corresponded, as you said just now, but I can't compare now because I don't have the other document. But you stated it correctly because we did analyse it during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Just a few more documents I want to look at now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a command of the Drina Corps 12 July 1995 document headed, "Very urgent." It will come up in a minute, sir, and I think this is one which you did not see Saturday, so take a moment to look at it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: That's true. I've not seen this document before. Let me just say that I saw some of the documents that you showed me during the proofing for the first time, save for those documents that I myself drafted in the Main Staff; and as for this document, we did not even discuss this document during the proofing, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Again, but, as with the previous documents of 12 July, this one, if you can read in your version, states that pursuant to the VRS General Staff commander's order to provide 50 buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave, and then it goes on talking about the types of fuel that will be allocated and the places the buses will come from. So is this related to the same operation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is probably related to the same operation. I cannot comment upon this document because this is really not within my purview. I did not deal with fuel and the petrol. But since a reference is made to the place from which the buses were requisitioned, I would say that this had to do with that document. And I apologise, let me dwell upon this document for just a brief moment. I don't know what document by the commander of the Republika Srpska army is referred to herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me go now to 65 ter number 871. Again, 12 July 1995, command of the Drina Corps document, headed, "Urgent." And it states that the topic is the provision of buses for the evacuation of the Srebrenica enclave, and it's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We did look at this Saturday, sir. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course, I recall that. I saw this document during proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, again, if you look at the second paragraph -- I'm sorry. It will be the first paragraph on your version, the first full paragraph after the distribution list. It states that all of the available buses and minibuses belonging to units of the RS, VRS, must be secured for the use of the Drina Corps and head towards the Sports Stadium in Bratunac on 12 July 1995. Is this --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Could I please see the addressee block? Thank you. It was sent to the command of the brigades that were on the strength of the Drina Corps. The only difference is specific of this document is that it says the buses owned by the units, which means that these buses were not requisitions. They were owned by the units already, and they served to transport their own men to the front lines and back from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But, again, according to this order, on this day, 12 July, 1995, they are going to Bratunac Sports Stadium, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: If that is how the document reads, then it must have been that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that how the document reads to you, or does it read some way different to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is exactly how the document reads: "Bratunac, the Sports Field."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And sorry, if we could just take a look at the number of this order, it's 22/226, and if we could now go to 02901 -- 02902, excuse me. I apologise. We do not yet have a translation of this document. This document is from the 5th Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, dated 12 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The only part I want you to look at, sir, is the bottom two lines of the second full paragraph. Forgive my pronunciation, it starts off "Vasje naredenje." Could you read that out to us, please? Yes. Where the cursor is.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can see that sentence starting with "Vase naredenje."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you read it, please, out loud?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The whole paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, just that last sentence, which has the date 12 July 1995 in it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: "Your order, strictly confidential number 22/226, dated 12 July 1995, was carried out in keeping with our capabilities."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So I think that speaks for itself, but this document, then, is connected to the previous document we looked at; is that -- do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Can we see the heading, please? This document was issued by the command of the 5th Light Infantry Brigade, which was subordinated to the command of the Drina Corps, and reported to the command of the Drina Corps on all the things stated herein, including the thing that you asked me to read. And can we now scroll up, please? Who signed it? I suppose it was the commander. Actually, it does say here the commander of that brigade. This was part of the regular procedure that was in place to provide for the communication between the commands. Whenever they received an order, they were supposed to report back on that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm done with that topic. I've got a new topic now, and I want to talk to you about any meetings you had on the 14th of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we have 02905 up, please? If we could scroll down to the entry for the 14th of July, this is an excerpt of the appointment calendar for Radovan Karadzic for 14 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you see your name on here, on the list of persons with appointments that day with Mr. Karadzic? I can help you. It says "12.15 to 12.35," fifth line down.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that. It is in the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you meet with Radovan Karadzic that day, 14 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I did. I met with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Why did you meet with him? What was the purpose? What was the topic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I went to see the president of the Republika Srpska because I had received an order to take to him the orders for the decorations that he was supposed to sign, and this is exactly what I did. I took those to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was anybody else present at the meeting with you and Dr. Karadzic on the 14th of July, around noon? Try to remember as best you can.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember, but I believe that only Bogdan Subotic was present. He was a general and a chief of the military part of the president's offers, and I really wouldn't be able to recall anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember a time when you thought there might have been somebody else present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness has already answered the question as to who was present during the meeting; in other words, this was asked and answered. The witness has already answered that, and my learned friend is repeating the same question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not the same question. I'm asking if a little while ago he had a - I am looking for my question - if he had a different view on who was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your previous question was: "okay. Now was anybody else present at the meeting with you and Dr. Karadzic on the 14th of July around noon? Try to remember best." He told you: "I can't remember, but I believe that only Bogdan Subotic," et cetera, et cetera," and I really wouldn't be able to recall anybody else. And your next question: "Okay. Do you remember a time when you thought there might have been somebody else present at that meeting?" So what you're being asked now is that perhaps now you don't recall anybody else being present at that meeting, but was there another occasion in the past when you did recall the presence of someone else and you said -- you said as much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have stated that General Gvero was also present at the meeting, but the following thing confused me: The President of Republika Srpska did mention General Gvero at that meeting in the sense that he had written a report which was detrimental to the morale of the Republika Srpska army. And this information has confused me, and I really can't claim that General Gvero was there. I can only say, upon reflection and based on logic, that what my job with the president was had nothing to do with what General Gvero had to deal with. So my conclusion would be that General Gvero probably was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to proceed to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, and it's something you talked about before: What other issues, beyond military issues which would fall directly within your competence, your mandate, were discussed at the meeting with Karadzic? You already started talking about morale reports, but what else was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I need to correct you here. I did not report to him about the state of morale. That was not within my purview. But the president said - and I paraphrase because I can't remember his words exactly - that he was not an old lady and that he would certainly remove General Gvero; that Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic, as far as I can remember - and this is what I said to Mr. McCloskey as well - had sold a tape; and he also mentioned a name that I don't want to mention because the person is deceased, and out of respect. He mentioned that name as well; and if you insist, Your Honours, I can say that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know that name so I don't know what could or could not be entailed. Mr. Nicholls, if you are aware of the name and you wish to pursue this line of questions, we can go in private session and he can mention the name in private session. I don't know if it's of any relevance or it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think at this point I can just continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Move on. Okay. Go ahead, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask this: Who drafted the morale reports you talked about a minute ago? Who would have drafted those reports?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What morale reports are you referring to? I don't understand your question. Are you talking about information about the state of morale? Is that what you're implying?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: They were drafted by the sector for Morale Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs, and they were sent to the units to inform them about the state of morale within the army of Republika Srpska, and that information was also sent to the corps. I don't know whether it was sent to the higher command unit, i.e. the supreme command. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall stating in your interview who you said probably spoke about morale issues at that meeting with Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: At the Office of the President, we did not go into any detail on that subject. The president himself told us that that alleged information was detrimental to the morale of the army, rather than being beneficial to it, and that he had corrected that. I don't know how he did that. I suppose that in that information - that's what I've already stated, and I repeat it today - one could read about the problems, especially problems in society, were exerting negative influence on the morale in the army, which I believe the president did not find very pleasant to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I don't think you understood my question. My question was other than you -- my question was who spoke about morale issues, not what those issues were and the long answer. And let me just ask you if you remember saying this in your interview. It's on page 39 of the English, page 38 of the Serbian: "Okay. So if you didn't speak to him about those morale issues, who did?" Your answer, this is about that same meeting: "Probably Gvero." Do you remember giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I do, and I can read it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, one moment Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask whether this cross-examination goes to the credibility of the witness or to the truth of the answer? Because if it's the former, then no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we should discuss this in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour. I'm just trying to help the witness -- I'm not -- it probably should not be discussed in front of the witness. You're right. But I don't know that we really need to get into a discussion about it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously, the witness understands English. So if you want to discuss it further, we need the witness to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If Mr. Nicholls is going to move on, I don't want to make a mountain out of a mole hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I am moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we look at 02648 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's a different topic now, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, actually, Your Honours, before I discuss this document, I guess I should -- I don't know if I can. This is a document that we had previously asked to have assigned a 65 ter number. That's referenced in the motion, and that decision is pending. The only purpose of this - and I think I can say this in front of the witness - is that it's the witness's document. He wrote it, which is why I wanted to show it to him, but I believe Your Honours, unless I'm wrong, have not yet made a decision on whether it can be added to the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the current motion that I told you, you should have filed -- we would have preferred to you file earlier or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. It's an earlier motion, Your Honour, from 6 July, which I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I have a list here of all pending motions. Just give me a moment. We have the Butler one, 26th. 6th of July, Prosecution filed a motion requesting leave to amend the 65 ter list with 18 exhibits pertaining to Alistair Graham.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that may not be it. This was -- this was sought to be admitted as corroboration for some of the intercept exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there was a 12th of July motion, still pending, requesting to supplement its 6th July motion. On 6th of July, Prosecution have a motion to amend the 65 ter list pertaining to intercept corroboration documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It would be one of -- that is the one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And this, obviously, we haven't decided upon because we are dealing with this matter together with the other issues related to intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll ask my friends if there is an objection. I simply want the witness to look at the document in order to help lay the foundation and authenticity of this document, even if it's not admitted at this time pending your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there anyone from the Defence teams that doesn't agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have just one question that I would like to clarify with my learned friend. According to the 65 ter list, a document that will be used for these documents, under the number, if the counsel could repeat the number. I have the document. I wonder whether the mistake is in the list or in the transcript, and are we talking about the same document? Because in the transcript, page 37, line 13, we have 02648. Could the counsel please repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this document is on the list for direct examination of this witness. I believe that the Defence has already objected to the admission of these documents on the list according to Rule 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that my friend has objected in the context of the motion that was filed first referring to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. What I was wondering is since we have the witness here, if I could show the document just to establish its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Independently and irrespective and without prejudice to your position taken vis-a-vis the 6th of July Prosecution motion, for the purpose of this witness, and for the purpose of establishing, it seems only, the authenticity of this document, do you have an objection for the use of this document with the present witness, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Got nothing to do with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were -- you wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've got no interest in this document. Others might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Anybody wishes to object to the limited use? We hear no objection, then you may proceed accordingly, and use of this document will not prejudice the pending issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could have 02468 up on the screen, please? And with the assistance of the usher, I have the original, if I could show it to the witness; and, perhaps, show it to my friend, if they want to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I showed you this document as well Saturday. Can you just tell me what that document is and whose signature is on it? That's all I'd ask from you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You've already showed me this document, the contents of which have reminded me of this document. The signature is by General Skrbic, which is myself, and the signature is absolutely authentic. The document speaks about sending two volunteers from Poland to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have no other questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Miletic does have questions for this witness, and we will seek to stay within our estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. My name is Nenad Petrusic, and I have some questions for you on behalf of the Defence of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Main Staff of the VRS, that command had already been completed in organisational and other terms, as you stated in your evidence earlier, and I would like to know whether this military establishment was set up in keeping with the constitution and the Law on the Armed Forces of Republika Srpska and the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The organisation of the entire army of Republika Srpska, including its Main Staff, was based on the constitution, the Law on Defence and the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, and the establishment for each organisational unit had been stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A lot of enactments, laws, and by-laws dealing with the organisation of the army had been taken over by the VRS from the JNA, just as by the other two armies?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could we then say that in July 1995, and in the course of the entire year 1995, the army of Republika Srpska was an organised and disciplined military establishment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I could agree about the organisation, but I cannot say anything about discipline. It is not such an easy matter that I could elaborate on here. I could not agree that it was completely disciplined, but it would require scientific analysis to prove the truth of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In any case, the principles of subordination and single command were observed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Up to the level of brigade, which I'm familiar with, formal relations prevailed in the VRS, that means subordination and single command in terms of personnel interrelations, but I cannot say anything about lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have 5438, Exhibit 5438 --.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P438.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D438.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, would you be able to follow this schematic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: With great difficulty because the letters are too small. But in my proofing with you, after the proofing with the Prosecution, I did see this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, can we agree that the commander -- that this is the composition of the Main Staff of the VRS in July 1995, as indicated on the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You mean in terms of names and surnames?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I mean organisationally and in terms of personnel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This schematic has nothing to do with the organisation as it was in July 1995. There are occasional similarities, but not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We'll come to the name and to the details, but I would like to know whether the commander of the Main Staff in this schematic is presented in the appropriate place here, in the proper place, in keeping with the organisation of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander is indicated in his right place but a small box is missing here, which may not be important because formally the military office of the commander of the Main Staff did not really exist, but it was envisaged by the establishment. So a small box should be there that has nothing to do with the subordinates down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, when you look at this schematic, please ignore the operative units below the command of the Main Staff. Look only at the command, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I hope that right next to you there is a pen that is able to write on the screen. Could you please look at this schematic and see if the position of Chief of Main Staff is correctly indicated?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you place the Chief of the Main Staff in the right place according to organisational structure? General, wait a minute. Wait until I've finished my question so that the interpreters can keep up; otherwise, the record will be a mess, and can you please take care to remember this in future?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So I'll repeat the question. Can you place the Chief of Main Staff in his right position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Then please draw it in, write the letters "NS" with a diacritic, to indicate the proper place of Manojlo Milovanovic, Chief of Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I understand you want to erase this first line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it technically possible to erase the first line, because I understand the general is trying to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Line erased] Can you erase this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we could say that the Chief of Staff was the Chief of the Staff Sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next box we see on the schematic, to the right of the first box, marked as The Staff, and you say that it's really the Staff Sector, is the Section for Air Force and Air Defence. Is the section properly placed in the schematic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ask the AV directors to zoom in on the central part of this schematic because that's the one we need.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We need to save this image if you want to keep it and then we can zoom in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be better, because I can't see. Where is this section in the schematic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To cut it short, let's save this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I see it now. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. But if I may be allowed to suggest something before we save this, may I ask the witness: Would it be correct to cross out the Chief of the Main Staff as he is represented originally?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, General, on this schematic, where you see the Chief of the Main Staff, could you cross that out with that red pen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There it is, because I put him in the proper place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let us also look on this schematic for the part where it says, "Staff," and could you correct that to read, "Staff Sector"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the right-hand corner, please write today's date, the 17th of September; and in the right-hand corner, place your initials.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks] Is this enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now save this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, save it. For the record, the date appears -- does not appear near the signature, but it's still visible on another part of the document. Yes. Now, if you could indicate which part of the same document you wish to refer the witness to, we can go straight to that part, and we can zoom in.
