utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The part of the schematic which is to the right of the date placed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, General, do you agree that the section of Air Force and Air Defence is properly placed in organisational terms?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, the name is not accurate, and its position on the schematic is not accurate. Can I tell you exactly what it was called?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Administration for Air Defence and Air Force. It's true that it was headed by Major General Jovo Maric. It's true that he was assistant commander for Air Force and Air Defence, and this box should be on the right end of this line, before the Administration for Planning, Development, and Finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All right. General. Let's go ahead. The Section for Intelligence and Security, is that one correctly positioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The name, again, is not correct. It's called Administration for Intelligence and Security. Sorry, let me repeat. It was called the sector for Intelligence and Security, without the J, which is in a different dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That sector had two administrations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The Administration for Security and the Administration for Intelligence; that is, the intelligence administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There was an intelligence administration, you put that correctly, but the other one was called Administration for Security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next organisational unit, according to this schematic, is the Section for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs; is that one correctly positioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Its place is proper. It's correct, but the name is not. It was called the sector for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs; and, again, it's a different dialect, with a J.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next sector or the next organisational structure or element is the Department for Replenishment and Personnel Affairs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This name is completely wrong. The name is Sector for the Organisation, Mobilisation, and Personnel Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If we go on, we can see the Department for Logistical Services. Is that name correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, it's not. The name is this: The Sector for the Rear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The next one is the Department for Development and Finances. Do we have another problem with the name?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. The problem is still the same. The name is not correct. The name was the Administration for the Planning of Development and Finances, and this was together with the administration that we have already mentioned, the Air Force and the Anti-Aircraft Defence, the only other independent administration at the sector level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you to zoom out this schematic that is on the screen now. Actually, can you blow up the whole image a little bit? We would still like to have the whole image on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, can you encircle the Staff Sector on this schematic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we zoom in a bit more, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, could you please encircle the Staff Sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks] I've done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you use a different colour, if there is one, and encircle the command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can't. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you encircle the command of the Main Staff? Could you encircle the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The whole schematic, save for the corps, is the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You want me to put a circle around it. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The position of the Chief of the Staff Sector, Manojlo Milovanovic, should this be at the head of the red circle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Not that it only should be, but it was at the head of that square. Would you like me to mark that? I'll do that if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No. This is enough for the record. In other words, the head of all the other sectors and the two administrations -- actually, the heads of all those were heads of sectors?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. Those were the assistant commanders of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army under establishment. That was not their official title. The only chief was the Chief of the Staff Sector. That was the only name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not trying to challenge your testimony, but we've heard some other officers here, among them Manojlo Milovanovic, who have told us that the heads of these sectors were chiefs who were also assistant Commanders. But at this point, this is not of much importance. What I'm going to ask you now is this: Did the Chief of the Staff Sector hold an equal footing with the other assistants of the commander, as you call them, or could one say that he was one among the equals --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Or that he was he was the first among the equals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the establishment, the Chief of the Staff Sector, who was also the deputy commander of the Main Staff, was at the same level with the other assistants. Your definition was correct when you said that he was the first among them, obviously, after the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's go back briefly to the Staff Sector. Will you agree with me if I put it to you that in that sector, there was an Administration for Operations and Training, and that the head of that administration, in July 1995, and the rest of 1995, was Colonel, later on General, Radivoje Miletic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is correct, yes. What you've just said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of his administration, if we want to call it that way, there were three departments: The training department, the operations department, and the operations centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Kindly do not make me analyse these lower levels because I don't remember. However, the way you described the composition is correct, but you did not mention the organs of the branches.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's take it easy, General. We will come to the branches in due course. I would just like to ask you to confirm that these three departments were indeed part of the Administration for Operations and Training, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Within the Staff Sector, there were also branch organs. Let's not go into any details of that. Could you please tell us or do you remember what branch organs were those? If you don't know, never mind.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember some. I'm not sure that I'll be able to remember all of them. Let's start with first things first: Infantry; armoured and mechanised units; artillery, engineers; the anti-aircraft units, i.e. the branch of service called the Anti-Aircraft Defence. Now, whether I've managed to remember all of them, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the Chief of the Staff Sector was the first superior to the organs and the branches of services, as well as to the Chief of the Administration for Operations and Training. In other words, Manojlo Milovanovic was their immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You've put it absolutely correctly. There is no need for me to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please put today's date in the lower right-hand corner of the schematic, General.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Also mark the schematic with your initials.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And now take the red pen and put the words "Staff Sector" above the red square.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: You want me to put in words what we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Above the red square, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: "MM."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: [Marks] "Chief, MM." S with the diacritic T is the abbreviation for the Staff Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's remove that from the e-court, and now I would like to call Exhibit 5D431.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you will agree with me, won't you, that this is or at least this is what it reads: "Establishment number 111.900," that this is personal material, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, 1993. This is what it reads: "Military secret, strictly confidential," and the record number is 1. Could you briefly tell us what is this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What I see in front of me is a copy of the first page or the title page of the book whose title you have just read out, and this is really an authentic copy. The word "Serbian" should be in capital letters. It should not be in minuscule.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2 of this document? Can you move the document a bit to the right; actually, to the left. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the title of this document, we can read as follows: "An overview of duties per units and establishment elements, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll up a little to show bullet point 10? Okay. Let's scroll down. Thank you. I apologise. Let's look at bullet points from 1 to 10. Can we please see entries from 1 to 10 on the screen? Scroll up the document, please, 1 to 10? That's enough. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, so you see that this is the establishment of the Main Staff. Under 1, we see the commander of the Main Staff, and 10 is the Chief of Staff. At the same time, we see in brackets, assistant commander -- sorry, deputy commander. So that is how it was envisaged also in 1995. Those were the establishment positions in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The establishment of the Main Staff did not change. That's how it was in 1995 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Look at number 10, that's staff. And under number 12, we see the Chief of the Administration for Operations and Training. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So we see that according to this schematic, the law maker did not envisage that the Chief of the Administration for Operations and Training would at the same time be deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There was no such possibility under the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. But the general rule is that every position in establishment should be supported by appropriate rules.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: We observed in practice their titles and positions in establishment. So if the chief of an administration was not intended to be a deputy, he was not called the deputy, and he was not the deputy. If I may clarify: When making appointments to this position - you see that this was a major general - it is done by decree. And this decree says that this person is appointed to be Chief of Operations and Training, and it is not mentioned anywhere that he would be a deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you know, and it is not contested, that General Milovanovic, as Chief of Staff of the VRS, spent a certain time in 1995 - we won't guess how much time - outside the command post in Crna Rijeka. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was replaced in that period by any superior officer, including Colonel, later General, Miletic? Was he represented by any officer, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I do know that General Milovanovic, Manojlo Milovanovic, was part of the army of Republika Srpska, and he was not absent from the army. As long as he was there, and he was not infirm or unable to perform his duties for objective reasons, nobody can replace him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would it then be fair to say that General Milovanovic - and we now know that he was at the forward command post of the Krajina Corps - in addition to his regular duties of Chief of Staff of the VRS, also discharged certain functions entrusted to him by, I suppose, the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The question was not quite clear, but I suppose that you mean he was given the duty to command part of our troops which were located in that part of the theatre of war, in the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But in addition to that duty that he was assigned, he continued to be Chief of Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: He remained the Chief of Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We have documentation, to be more precise daily combat reports of the Main Staff of the VRS, addressed to the Supreme Command and to subordinate units signed by Colonel, later General, Miletic; and above his signature, we see, "Replacing the Chiefs of Staff" [as interpreted]. If General Miletic had been appointed as representative or replacement for the Chief of Staff, would that enactment, would that appointment, have had to go through your sector? Would you have had to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer that question, yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if my friend finished his question but the wording is important here. I'd rather we see the document in the original language that he's referring to, rather than worry about any shading of the words in translation into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think the point made by Mr. Nicholls is very pertinent, a very pertinent one. I don't know what to suggest to you, but perhaps you can refer straight to the document you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have this document, and I can give it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put it in e-court, as my colleague suggests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P48.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can do that. I was just alerted to a possible error in the transcript. It says in English that my friend's question was at line 6 of the previous page, "We see: 'Replacing the Chiefs of Staff,'" and I'm told what my friend said was "Standing in for Chiefs of Staff," which I won't comment on that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that as well. So we have the document now on the screen. I don't know if the witness can see it. I think he should be able to see it. Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Go ahead with your question. Perhaps it would be better if you repeated it. And I would enjoin the interpreters to ensure that we have a correct translation of the precise words used by Mr. Petrusic in his question. Go ahead, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, could you look at this front page? In the heading, we see, "the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, strictly confidential, 03/3-234, date 22 August."

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't have that document on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My mistake. I was looking at a different document. I'm sorry. So we see, "Main Staff of the VRS, strictly confidential number 03/3-195, date 14 July 1995. Very urgent. To the president of Republika Srpska, to the commands of ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you need to read them all. Shall we go straight to the bottom part of the document, where there is his signature, and I think we need to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Mr. President. So the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to go to the next page or the last page any way, where we see his signature. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you see this document was issued by Radivoje Miletic, and it says, "Acting on behalf [as interpreted] of the Chief of Staff, Major General Radivoje Miletic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry. It's not an objection. I'm told it's another error in the translation. Again, it was: Standing in for the Chief of Staff," which is what he said. Maybe he can tell us, and the translation is coming as something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would leave it. For the witness, it's not relevant for the time being, because he can see the words over there. Yes, Madam Fauveau? Yes, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry to intervene. But since it is a linguistic problem, I do prefer to speak for myself. I believe the interpreters-- I think we have excellent interpreters here, and they see very well what is written on the document. So if they interpreted in that way, it must be a possible interpretation or translation of this document. I don't know how the Prosecutor can insist on standing in, because I believe that the Prosecution bench is not really bilingual in B/C/S and English, and I would give credence to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau and Mr. Nicholls. I think this whole business can be proceeded with and cleared up through the questions that Mr. Petrusic will be putting to the witness. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, did a request ever reach your sector to appoint General Miletic representative of the Chief of Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: There was no such request and there was no such order ever written; therefore, General Miletic never represented anyone by virtue of an order because such an order did not exist. And if you allow me to add, it is correctly written on this copy that he is representing or acting on behalf, but it's not correctly written. What should have been written is "Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel Milovanovic"; and then, Mr. Miletic, who was probably told by Milovanovic, "Sign some documents for me, please," should have put the word "Za," meaning in English, "For," in front of Milovanovic's name before signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So Milovanovic could have told General Miletic to go on and sign some documents on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: General Miletic would not have done it without the permission of General Milovanovic, but Milovanovic probably instructed him what he may and may not sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So these combat reports, be they daily or interim, addressed to the president of the state and subordinate commands, fall within those documents that General Miletic was allowed to sign on the authority of his own superior, Chief of Staff Manojlo Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really answer that question. It's obvious that he did sign. These seem to be regular, daily reports, and they do contain important information. But since they are done routinely, then I suppose General Milovanovic authorised General Miletic to sign them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could we say, then, that for the purposes of regular functioning of the staff during the day, certain documents should be put out from that staff, documents that are not that important and could be signed by General Miletic? Would it be fair to say that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Such documents he was able to sign, General Miletic, I mean. But he could not have signed important documents without consulting General Milovanovic, so he had to make a phone call; and even in those cases, when Milovanovic would tell him, "Go ahead, sign," he could sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So General Milovanovic would have received each of those reports at his forward command post and he would have been aware, and he would have seen, that the document was going to be signed or was signed by General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Since I'm not sure, how can I answer that question? Could you bring back the page with the heading so that I see where it was sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 1, please, again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It says, "IKM," meaning forward command post, "-2," and that's where General Milovanovic was. So he knew about this document and he knew who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And he would have been able to object to this signature at this document, or on any other document, if he had not authorised General Miletic to represent him in regular staff duties?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course, he was able to object because he was the superior, but he didn't need to object in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a short break of 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we now have in e-court 5D447?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document from the Main Staff of the VRS, signed by the Chief of Staff, Lieutenant-Colonel General Manojlo Milovanovic. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you please read it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You will agree that briefly this document concerns a transfer of troops from the 65th Protection Regiment to the Drina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The document was issued on the 21st August 1995. Could we say that this document is one of the regular documents necessary for the functioning of the staff? Or to put it more simply, is this the kind of document that could be written by General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Not even General Manojlo Milovanovic should have signed this. I was the one who should have signed because that was my job. If you remember, this number, 09, is the number indicating the sector that I belonged to. It's possible that I was not present and this needed to be dealt with urgently, and then General Manojlo Milovanovic signed. That's as far as I remember. We had lots of problems at the time at the western part of the theatre of war, and we were all there, but not all of us in one location; and when I say "we," I mean generals belonging to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was together with you, or rather, you were together with him on the western theatre of war, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for clarity, what time period are we talking about? Just the date of this document, or is he -- it's a general question he's asked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, fair comment [Realtime transcript read in error "meant"]. Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about this date, 21st August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, line 16, I didn't say, "Yes, fair meant." I said, "fair comment." I think once you have mentioned the date, you need to go back to the witness and ask him to confirm whether the information he gave in reply to your previous question is precise, is correct, applies as well to the 21st of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, you heard the suggestion of His Honour the Presiding Judge. What we said earlier about this information and the presence of you and General Milovanovic, does that apply to the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When I was answering, I meant only this day, the 21st August 1995, because I remember clearly that we were in the western theatre of war. But whether we were together or not, I cannot recall. When I say "together," I mean in the same location, but we were both certainly in the western theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So from that forward command post of the Main Staff, General Milovanovic had the ability to use radio relay communications, teleprinters, and all the prerogatives of the command; and when I say, "prerogatives," I mean code numbers and reference numbers and everything else we see in the heading of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: For as long as radio relay communications were not destroyed by air strikes, he had the ability to use them in any part of the theatre of war controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To avoid confusion about the period, since you mentioned air strikes, which period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The year 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And when were communications destroyed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I believe towards the end of 1995, just before the Dayton Accords. Almost all of our radio communications were destroyed. On this date, however, they were still working because this was sent by teletype.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And if a document of this kind had reached your sector, signed by General Miletic, what would you have done?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have suggested to him that he shouldn't do that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would read what it was about. Since this is about a transfer of troops, I would have forgiven him, of course. I mean, in any case, I would not have punished him or anything. It was not my responsibility, but I would tell any other colleague not to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was General Miletic able to issue any orders to you? And I'm talking about orders.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: General Miletic was never able to give me orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was he able to coordinate the work of the command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: In my understanding of the word "coordinate," he was not able to do that. If you meant something different, then you can rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, did you have regular collegium meetings? Are you familiar with the term? If you did, can you tell me something about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We did hold Sector Staff meetings up to the 15th of January 1996. All of these were extraordinary meetings of the collegium of the Main Staff. It was only in 1996, when we had peace, we had regular meetings. During the war, we did not have regular meetings. We met on an ad hoc basis. Most of the meetings that had to be held were relative to the personnel issues, when we had to discuss promotions, appointments, decorations. I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you use the term "we," who do you mean? Who were members of this Sector Staff or the collegium?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to -- I apologise. Do you want me to give you their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: First of all, can you confirm whether there was an inner collegium and a broader collegium?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who were members of the inner collegium or the inner Sector Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army, the Chief of the Sector Staff, and all the assistants. Those were the members of the inner collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say "assistants," are you referring to the assistants to the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I mean the assistants to the commander of the Main Staff for Intelligence and Security matters, for Organisation and Mobilisation, for Logistics, for Air Force and the Anti-Aircraft Defence, and the assistant for Planning and Finances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who the members of the broader collegium were. In order to save time, you don't have to give us any of their names.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Those were the corps commanders of all the corps; the commander of Air Force and Anti-Aircraft Defence; and, as needed, some commanders of the independent units that belonged to the Main Staff; for example, the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call Exhibit 5? That is 0005 into e-court. That is P5, document P5. In order to speed the matters up, I would kindly ask the usher to give the document in hard copy to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, in short, you can see that this -- are you going to confirm that this is Directive Number 7 issued by the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, signed by the Supreme Commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic? Please look at the last page where it is stated that the directive was drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic. The date is 8 March 1995. Do you agree that we can find this in the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I am looking at the copy, at the hard copy of the document, and I can also see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at number 1. The title is, "Basic Characteristics of the International Military and Political Situation." And then on page 2, in the Serbian version that you have in your hand, it says, "Croatian and Muslim coalition forces." General, do you agree that these two bullet points or these two paragraphs were written in the present form in the Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they were drafted, but it says here that the document was drafted by General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This is beyond dispute?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know where this was written, and let me add to this. I saw this directive for the first time on 12 May 2005 when Mr. McCloskey showed it to me. Is my pronunciation of this name correct, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I will agree with you that you saw this directive for the first time at that moment, but you said on that occasion that you and your sector were -- had not been asked to provide any input where the directive was being drafted. My question is this: The person who drafted the directive, in this case, Colonel Miletic, did he approach various sectors in order to ask for their input? This is my question to you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: If the commander of the Main Staff had issued an order to him to consult particular sectors and to ask for their input, then he was duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether paragraphs 1 and 2, in respect of their contents, could only have been supplied by the Intelligence and Security Sector, in light of the fact that these paragraphs speak about the strength of the enemy. And you know only too well that the enemy was within the purview of the intelligence department, first and foremost.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Based on my military knowledge, or general military knowledge, and de facto, I assume that nobody else could have provided this input, save for the sector, because this type of information and data is accessible only to that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And that sector should have provided that information to Colonel Miletic, judging by what is indicated on the last page of the directive under the word "drafted by"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I don't know whether they provided any information or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at paragraph number 3? I repeat, this is a directive issued by the Supreme Command, by the president of the republic; and under item 3, he issues tasks to the army of Republika Srpska. I am now referring to a general military knowledge, and I'm asking you whether this task could -- was phrased by the then Supreme Commander, Dr. Karadzic, in light of the fact that this task was given to the entire military.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Bullet point 3 must be phrased by the person who signed such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In that case, we will agree that it was President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was the Supreme Commander. He signed this decision, which means that he was the one who worded items 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And now if we move to bullet point 5 on page 7, you can see that this bullet point contains tasks given to particular units. Can you see the title, "Tasks to the units" on the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So these are the tasks issued to subordinated units, is that correct, to the subordinated units, i.e., operative groups; in this particular case, the 2nd Krajina Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, and so on and so forth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: To all the corps, including the Sarajevo Corps, which you did not mention, the Air Force, the Anti-Aircraft Defence, and the Central Military Schools as a combat part of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, the tasks of these operational units was given by the commander of the General Staff Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was it who gave out those tasks?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It was the Supreme Commander of the army of Republika Srpska, President Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to bullet point 6 on page 10 in the Serbian version: "Support to combat activities." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to your military knowledge, who would it have been to draft this bullet point? In other words, which sector would be dealing with the issues in this bullet point?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you bear with me while I read the text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could I ask my friend to break that question up, because it's who would draft it and who would deal with it. There are names on this document as drafters, and he is asking, I think, about something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair comment. General, you have heard Mr. Nicholls. Perhaps you can do the exercise yourself. First, who would have drafted this bullet point, to use the same words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was drafted by the person indicated herein, Colonel Radivoje Miletic. So he was the one who drafted this bullet point as well, the bullet point that we are talking about, number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And who have dealt with it, with the issues mentioned in these -- in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morale and psychological preparations were within the purview of the Sector for Moral Guidance and Legal Matters. However, I have read the text in order to be able to tell you this: This phrase could have been copied from any document, even from literature on morale and psychological preparations of fighters for an operation, for a mission at hand, and so on and so forth. It would have been within the authority of the sector that I've just mentioned. But who it was that submitted information to General Miletic, I really wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, I will not go into any details, in this bullet point or any other for that matter. That was not my intention in the first place, but I would like to say or suggest to you that a document was prepared in this way, i.e. that all the sectors did what they were supposed to do, that the information was collected by Colonel Miletic, and then that he gave the document the form that you have in front of you and entitled it, "Directive number 7." And after this form was produced, this document went for signature to Dr. Radovan Karadzic, who could have signed it or refused to sign it or asked for some amendments. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the wording of all bullet points in this directive, according to my general knowledge, and particularly bullet points from 3 to 7, the responsibility lies with the signatory, i.e. The Supreme Command of the army of Republika Srpska, the President of Republika Srpska ..." [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, we got stuck here. I'll read to you what we have and then you complete your answer, because the last part of your answer was not taken up and translated to us. "When it comes to the wording of all bullet points in this directive, according to my general knowledge, and particularly bullet point 3 to 5, the responsibility lies with the signatory; that is, the Supreme Commander of the army of Republika Srpska, the President of Republika Srpska," and then you said something else but it never showed up in the transcript. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember what I said. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. I wouldn't interfere here because you did ask a question before. Perhaps you could either repeat it all or repeat part of it. I don't know. I don't want to interfere with the way you wish to conduct your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be for the most part an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, when you look at this document, to the best of your military knowledge, is the document deficient in any way? Is something missing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is a copy. The document itself, in view of the degree of confidentiality indicated, which is written in the right-hand corner in the first page, "National Defence, State Secret," had to be verified by a stamp on each page. That is the main objection to this document from the point of view of military rules. I don't know if there is something wrong with this copy, or maybe the document was done without the stamp. God knows. Look at point 6. There is 6.2 -- sorry, there is 6.1, but where is 6.2? If you mark a paragraph with 6.1, there should be 6.2, and there is none.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that it was possible for some pages to be forged or torn out of this directive?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. I couldn't answer. I cannot suppose what happened. I can only tell you what is wrong from the point of view of methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now, in the light of this directive and its paragraphs 1 to 7, I believe we've gone through them all, which item was written by then Lieutenant Miletic? Is there an item written by Miletic himself?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, he wrote them all, but none of them are within his jurisdiction. He was just a technical person. He was the signatory; and if the signatory had any objections, they would have to return the document to Miletic to make the corrections. That's the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And who is able to make corrections and return the directive?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS had to review this document before the president signed it, but sometimes the president signed even though the commander of the Main Staff wasn't aware of it, and I don't know whether the commander of the Main Staff had reviewed this or not. However, when the president looked at this directive before signing it, he could have said, "This is all wrong," and he could have returned it, then he would have been able to say exactly how it should read, and then the person in charge of the drafting would redraft it and take it back to the signatory. As long as the signatory is not happy, he does not have to put his signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, since this document is marked "State Secret," who took to directive to Karadzic? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court again 5D431; second page, please. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, General, we are looking, again, at the establishment of the Main Staff of the VRS, and you will see under 5: "Chief of the Section for Communication or liaison with Foreign Military Representatives." In that section, was this chief or liaison Colonel Milos Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the first chief of that section was Colonel Vidoje Magazin, to be later replaced by Colonel Milos Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have P33?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So, this general -- this document is dated 9 July 1995, issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, the army of Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- signed by assistant commander Major General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the top again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Tell me, General, where did this document originate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: What do you mean where did it originate? It's obvious, the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I meant this number, 09. Is it 09?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: It's not 09.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How about number 12? Is that the Staff Sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: Each sector had its number. Mine was 09. The Staff Sector was 03. But in view of the fact that - and if you would raise it a bit, please, lift the document - you see that it's signed by assistant commander Major General Tolimir, I conclude that this number belongs to the Sector for Intelligence and Security. With your leave, Your Honours, I only remember the numbers of the Staff Sector and my own sector. They are the only ones I know by heart. I don't know about the numbers of the other sectors, so I had to infer that this is the number of the Intelligence and Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As of 1993, you were in the Personnel Sector of the Main Staff. From that time until the end of the war, do you know whether a representative of the Chief of Staff had ever been appointed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was in the Main Staff beginning with 1994 until the end of the war. In that time, not a single order on representation was written. If it had been written according to the rules of interrelations within the staff, it would have had to be written in the sector in which I was assistant commander, but I have never seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether General Miletic was ever absent in July 1995 from the command post and, specifically, whether he had travelled to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he went at that time. I don't know where he was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you don't know whether he was absent from the command post?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC
utterances.text: I don't know either way. His location was in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's true that some time is left, maybe one minute, until the official end of our time today, but I would like to finish here. It's possible that I will not have any questions left for tomorrow, or I will perhaps have only one or two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I make a correction, Your Honour, because I'm afraid the record will not reflect my words precisely and correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I take it you are reading through the English transcript, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I'm sorry if I pronounce badly in English [In English]: "Don't know either way his location was in Crna Rijeka." [Interpretation] I wasn't saying that he was in Crna Rijeka at that time, at that moment. I am saying that he was located in Crna Rijeka throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Before we adjourn, Mr. Krgovic or Mr. Josse, will you be cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for how long?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One hour at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One hour at least. And Mr. Sarapa?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I will have questions; although, it depends on the cross-examinations to follow. But I don't plan any at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll meet again tomorrow morning. General, between now and then, please make sure that you don't discuss with anyone or allow anyone to discuss with you the subject matter of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
